Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

Recent findings suggest that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

Industry observers note that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that the screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics firm. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

Sources indicate that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” claims Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Sources indicate that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

It has been revealed that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Sources indicate that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

In a recent development, sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

According to recent reports, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

In a recent development, this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga notes. “It was just substantial enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

In a recent development, dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

It has been revealed that but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Industry observers note that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

Industry observers note that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

In a recent development, “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Industry observers note that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson claims. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Recent findings suggest that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

In a recent development, after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

According to recent reports, absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

In a recent development, noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Sources indicate that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more vital than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

It has been revealed that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” notes neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

According to recent reports, medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

According to recent reports, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu claims.

Sources indicate that medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

According to recent reports, telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra indicates, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

Industry observers note that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

According to recent reports, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell states. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

In a recent development, the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as swiftly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell states. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In a recent development, in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in upcoming funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he states. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Industry observers note that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How promptly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Industry observers note that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person organization into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Recent findings suggest that luca Guadagnino has to return some videotapes. The Oscar-nominated director is passing on Scott Z. Burns‘ American Psycho adaptation.

“Scott Z. Burns wrote a fantastic script,” stated Guadagnino. “Unfortunately for me, as we speak, it’s not happening.”.

Industry observers note that in October 2024, Deadline revealed that Guadagnino was in final talks with Lionsgate to direct Burns’ adaptation, which would be produced by Frenesy Films, and executive produced by Sam Pressman, the son of Edward R. But in February, Ellis claimed that multiple high-profile actors “have turned it down,” adding that Burns had since completed a upcoming draft after the unnamed talent passed on the previous version.

Ellis teased that the film would be “completely different” from Mary Harron’s 2000 adaptation of American Psycho, which starred Christian Bale as homicidal investment banker Patrick Bateman, the literary character that Ellis created as a satirical take on masculinity. The Harron-helmed adaptation also starred Justin Theroux, Josh Lucas, Chloë Sevigny, Reese Witherspoon, Jared Leto, Willem Dafoe and more.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Industry observers note that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

According to recent reports, this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (484 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Revyl

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I began to notice a pattern of patterns in today’s age, which has had me thinking ever since.
  • As the volume of agent work explodes, engineering leverage will concentrate in two areas.
  • ⟣ Verification engineering ⟢ (closing the loop): building the tools, systems, and processes that can reliably establish whether a change meets its intended requirements, and produce actionable evidence and signals when it doesn’t.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I began to notice a pattern of patterns in today’s age, which has had me thinking ever since.

As the volume of agent work explodes, engineering leverage will concentrate in two areas. One is already getting attention, the other is less clearly named.

⟣ Verification engineering ⟢ (closing the loop): building the tools, systems, and processes that can reliably establish whether a change meets its intended requirements, and produce actionable evidence and signals when it doesn’t.

⟣ Pattern engineering ⟢ (shaping the loops): designing, curating, and reinforcing the conventions, abstractions, tools, and context that improve subsequent work across a codebase and company.

These practices have always mattered, but agents change how frequently those decisions get applied. They repeatedly learn from and extend the patterns already present in a codebase. A good pattern can improve thousands of subsequent changes, while a bad one can repeatedly steer work in the wrong direction.

Pattern engineering means removing sources of recurring misdirection: unit tests that lock in implementation details, stale architecture specs, unclear service ownership. It also means making good work easier: enforcing clear architectural boundaries, making good observability and tracing automatic through shared abstractions, and establishing which context is worth preserving, where it belongs, and when it needs updating.

One pattern that has served our engineering team very well: a single reliable way for a human or cloud agent to configure secrets, run your stack, and test a change in any supported development environment.

Sources indicate that A work trial candidate on a fresh Mac and a cloud agent should follow the same setup workflow, with no undocumented steps. Once dependencies and access are provisioned, you should have a running stack in under a minute.

And that workflow should stay current as engineers and their agents add services. It should derive from the same service definitions they already maintain, so supporting a new service doesn’t require someone to remember to patch a separate setup system. Every new engineer and agent benefits from that work, and every new service extends it.

revup, the CLI we use to set up every engineer's and agent's machine at Revyl.

21020100machines, one command, the same stack.

Recent findings suggest that I think of people like @poteto and @dexhorthy as pattern engineers. Their work turns engineering judgment into principles and workflows that other people and agents can reuse. pstack turns engineering patterns, including verification itself, into reusable agent skills. That’s what makes it so useful. It’s a crash course in pattern engineering with the batteries included.

Now put two companies with access to an unlimited array of agents side by side.

One repeatedly spends time trying to rediscover setup, correcting the same mistakes, figuring out whether work is done. The other turns those lessons into reliable tools, defaults, and verification pipelines.

As the volume of agent work grows, that difference compounds massively. The best teams know where to invest.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Jack Delaney – Updated Nov 21, 2026 at 5:16PM EST.
  • Long-term investors view broad market sell-offs as offering discounts on growth stocks.
  • Dutch Bros operates a rapidly expanding network of drive-thru coffee shops, while Celsius markets functional energy drinks through global retail channels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jack Delaney – Updated Nov 21, 2026 at 5:16PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Dutch Bros ›.

Long-term investors view broad market sell-offs as offering discounts on growth stocks. That's because, over the long run, stock prices tend to go up. So even amid some general uncertainty now, there could be good deals. Two such stocks we'll look at today are Dutch Bros (BROS -4.01%) and Celsius (CELH -7.36%).

Dutch Bros operates a rapidly expanding network of drive-thru coffee shops, while Celsius markets functional energy drinks through global retail channels. Both companies are disruptors in the competitive beverage stocks landscape. This comparison looks at their growth trajectories and financial health to help you decide which stock fits your strategy.

Dutch Bros operates a high-growth model focusing on drive-thru shops that serve a variety of hand-crafted beverages. The menu includes coffee, tea, lemonade, and the popular Dutch Bros Rebel energy drink. As of June 2026, the company managed over 1,200 locations in nearly 30 states. Customer concentration is a factor to watch, as the company's brand recognition is somewhat limited.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $2 billion. This represented a revenue growth rate of roughly 30.7% compared to the prior year period. The tech giant reported a net income of approximately $102 million during this same timeframe. This growth is driven by both fresh shop openings and steady traffic at existing locations.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

According to recent reports, celsius creates and markets functional beverages that have gained significant popularity in the U.S. and international markets. Its portfolio includes brands like CELSIUS and Alani Nu, sold through convenience stores, fitness centers, and large retailers. The company is substantially reliant on PepsiCo (PEP +1.11%) as its primary distributor in the U.S. and Canada. This single customer accounted for over 43% of revenue in 2025, and such high customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

Sources indicate that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue for the company reached roughly $3.2 billion. This reflects significant momentum with revenue growth of approximately 49.1% over the preceding year. During this timeframe, the company generated net income of nearly $230 million.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

According to recent reports, dutch Bros faces intense competition from established coffee chains and other quick-service restaurants. Its high geographic concentration in the Western U.S. remains a concern, as most of its shops are located in that region. Rapid expansion also carries risks of identifying suitable real estate and maintaining its unique corporate culture. Regulatory changes regarding labor laws or potential drive-thru bans in specific municipalities could impact its operational model.

Celsius is heavily dependent on its distribution agreement with Pepsi, which provides the backbone of its retail reach. This relationship creates potential conflicts of interest since Pepsi holds a significant ownership stake and board representation. The company also faces fierce competition from global players such as Monster Beverage (MNST -0.57%) and Red Bull. Additionally, integrating recent acquisitions like Alani Nu and Rockstar presents ongoing execution risks for the management team.

Celsius appears more attractively valued than Dutch Bros, as it offers a lower earnings multiple despite maintaining a significantly faster revenue growth rate.

Recent findings suggest that for investors taking the long view, broad market dips offer buying opportunities. After all, Dutch Bros opened at $35.50 on Nov. 16 and closed at $32.78 on Nov. 20. Celsius also saw its stock price dip, opening at $32.47 on Nov. 16 and closing at $28.46 by Nov. 20.

Choosing between the two growth stocks for a portfolio, however, I would rather own Dutch Bros.

One of the key reasons is that, as a growth stock, Celsius appears to be increasingly relying on acquisitions. In the third quarter of 2026, revenue for its CELSIUS brand fell by approximately 6%, and U.S. retail sales fell by 7%. It saw strong growth through its acquired Alani Nu brand, with revenue climbing 24% and retail sales growing 57.9%.

In comparison, in its third quarter, Dutch Bros grew revenue by nearly 30%, same-shop sales increased by 5.4%, and customer traffic grew by 1%. Granted, it's not an apples-to-apples comparison, given the differences in how the businesses operate. Still, it demonstrates that the growth opportunities for Dutch Bros come through its core offerings, as its stores are attracting more customers, selling more, and have future sales growth opportunities through newly introduced store openings.

While Celsius is buying growth, Dutch Bros is creating it. That makes Dutch Bros the stock I would want to buy for the long term, using sell-offs to pick up shares at a discount to where they could be trading in the future.

It has been revealed that white was the most popular car color 30 years ago and it maintains that ranking today. When combined with the prominence of black (23.4%) and gray (22.9%), the top three most popular colors hold 72% of market share for modern car colors. It’s worth noting that silver, the fourth grayscale color, has gained just over 1 percentage point in popularity over the past 30 years, moving from 7.3% to 8.4% market share since 1996. Silver now trails blue, which holds 9.1% market share. Most Popular Car Colors by Market Share: 2025 vs. 1996 - iSeeCars Study Rank Color 2025 1996 % Change 1 White 25.7% 22.1% 16.7% 2 Black 23.4% 14.2% 64.5% 3 Gray 22.9% 3.6% 528.4% 4 Blue 9.1% 10.2% -10.8% 5 Silver 8.4% 7.3% 14.3% 6 Red 7.0% 20.1% -65.2% 7 Green 2.2% 13.4% -83.8% 8 Brown 0.4% 2.9% -84.6% 9 Beige 0.4% 1.6% -73.8% 10 Orange 0.3% 0.2% 2.5% 11 Yellow 0.1% 0.3% -59.4% 12 Gold 0.0% 2.3% -98.1% 13 Purple 0.0% 0.7% -94.7% Grayscale colors* 80.4% 47.3% 70.1% Non-grayscale colors 19.6% 51.7% -62.2% *Grayscale colors are black, gray, silver, and white.

iSeeCars analyzed the colors of over 22 million used cars from model years 1996 - 2025 sold from January 2025 to May 2026 to determine the market share for each color.

Gray followed a different path, increasing in market share consistently through the entire period, ultimately rising from only 3.6% to 22.9% and nearly matching black.

In a recent development, black and white, which were always popular colors, also gained substantial market share, with black’s popularity growing mostly in the early 2000s’ model years and white gaining share starting in the 2010 model year. Conversely, red and green, which ranked as the 2nd and 4th most popular colors in the 1996 model year, declined substantially throughout much of the 30-year period, with each color’s market share now in single digits. Most other colors either lost what little market share they had or maintained their relatively low popularity. Orange was the only non-grayscale color to increase in popularity, though it remains rare at just 0.3% market share.

“The rise of grayscale cars had to come from somewhere, and it was primarily the fall of red and green, though nearly every non-grayscale shade has lost ground since 1996,” said Brauer.

“Trucks are seeing much more than a touch of gray, with the segment going from less than 1 gray truck in 20 in 1996 to 1 in 5 today,” noted Brauer.

“SUV market share has grown more than any other vehicle segment since 1996, but SUV color diversity went the opposite direction during that timeframe,” said Brauer.

“Gray has gained ground in every vehicle segment, and it’s the most dominant color for today’s passenger cars,” noted Brauer.

“Relative to every other vehicle segment, sports cars still offer a veritable rainbow of color diversity, illustrating the expressive nature of these vehicles and their owners,” stated Brauer.

iSeeCars analyzed the colors of over 22 million used cars from model years 1996 - 2025 sold from January 2025 to May 2026. The share of each color within each model year was calculated, as was the difference in share between model years 1996 and 2025.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that upcoming job listings on Apple’s website indicate the manufacturer’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the organization has also introduced upcoming restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give users more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

According to recent reports, over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted latest job listings that offer a closer look at its prepares to develop autonomous AI agents:.

In one, Apple stated it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

According to recent reports, today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring people to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the tech giant could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the fresh job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its prepares for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how swiftly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally rolled out its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the company is now rolling out the public beta for consumers looking to try the new features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with fresh privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several newly introduced features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

In a recent development, and speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful update, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and users on the public beta can now try out these upcoming features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

10 stocks we like better than Kraft Heinz ›.

Should everyday investors favor a turnaround value play or a reliable beverage leader? This match-up explores whether Kraft Heinz (KHC +1.89%) or Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%) is the better buy for your portfolio heading into 2027.

Both companies provide essential products that often resist economic downturns, yet they follow very different growth paths and valuation models today. This comparison breaks down their latest financial results and potential risks to help you make an informed decision.

Kraft Heinz produces and markets a massive global portfolio of branded foods and condiments, ranging from its namesake ketchup to Philadelphia cream cheese. As one of the prominent consumer staples stocks, it sells its products in more than 40 countries through retail and foodservice channels. Its largest customer is Walmart (WMT +1.51%), which accounts for approximately 21% of net sales, and this customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

Sources indicate that in the 12 months ended Sept. 26, 2026, revenue reached nearly $24.8 billion, representing a slight decline of approximately 1.5% compared to the prior period. The tech giant reported a net loss of roughly $3.5 billion during this timeframe, and its net margin was approximately -14%. These results reflect a period of adjustment as the company manages its global portfolio and navigates changing retail demand.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

In a recent development, coca-Cola is a global beverage powerhouse that owns or licenses hundreds of brands across categories like sparkling soft drinks, sports drinks, and juices. The company utilizes a vast network of independent bottling partners, including Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP +0.72%) and Coca-Cola HBC (CCHBF +0.67%), to distribute its products in over 200 countries. It recently secured an exclusive pouring rights agreement with KFC U.S. starting in January 2027.

Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Oct. 2, 2026, revenue reached approximately $51.1 billion, which represents a healthy growth of roughly 7.1% over the prior year. The company delivered net income of $14.6 billion, resulting in a strong net margin of about 28.7%. This profitability highlights the strength of its brands and its ability to maintain pricing power in various global markets.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

In a recent development, kraft Heinz faces intense competition from both major branded rivals, such as PepsiCo (PEP +1.11%) and Nestlé (NSRGF +1.24%), and low-cost private-label products. The company must constantly adapt to rapidly changing consumer preferences and is dependent on key retail customers, who may reduce shelf space or pricing leverage. Additionally, supply chain volatility and potential future impairments of its intangible assets remain significant concerns for the business.

Recent findings suggest that coca-Cola is exposed to risks from unfavorable global economic and geopolitical conditions that can impact its international operations. The company also faces health-related concerns regarding sweetened beverages, which often lead to increased regulatory scrutiny and shifts in consumer habits. Furthermore, Coca-Cola depends heavily on independent bottling partners and must navigate challenges like water scarcity and maintaining its brand image in a competitive landscape against PepsiCo and Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP +1.25%).

Kraft Heinz at the moment looks cheaper based on its much lower forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio and price-to-sales (P/S) ratio, suggesting it is priced as a value stock compared to Coca-Cola.

In a recent development, between the two, I favor Coca-Cola more for a simple reason: Kraft Heinz is executing a turnaround, while Coca-Cola is just executing.Looking at its recent performance for the third quarter of 2026, unit case volume grew 5%, organic revenue grew 7%, comparable earnings per share (EPS) grew 11%, and operating income grew 12%. But it's also seeing even larger volume growth with tweaks to its classic formulas, with Coca-Cola Zero Sugar volume growing 16%. To finish out the year, Coca-Cola's management expects 5% organic revenue growth and 11% comparable EPS growth.

While Kraft Heinz needs to show investors it can earn their confidence back, Coca-Cola has already earned the confidence. It just needs to keep executing from here.
